claim: In adult mammals, spermatogenesis embodies the complex developmental process from spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) to spermatozoa.
source: In adult mammals, spermatogenesis embodies the complex developmental process from spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) to spermatozoa.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about spermatogenesis.

claim: FOXC2 marks a quiescent adult SSC subpopulation in both mice and humans.
source: Using single-cell analysis and lineage tracing, we discovered both in mice and humans the quiescent adult SSC subpopulation marked specifically by forkhead box protein C2 (FOXC2).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell analysis and lineage tracing experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: All spermatogenic progenies can be derived from FOXC2+ SSCs.
source: All spermatogenic progenies can be derived from FOXC2+ SSCs and the ablation of FOXC2+ SSCs led to the depletion of the undifferentiated spermatogonia pool.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments showing FOXC2+ cells give rise to all spermatogenic cell types.

claim: Ablation of FOXC2+ SSCs led to the depletion of the undifferentiated spermatogonia pool.
source: All spermatogenic progenies can be derived from FOXC2+ SSCs and the ablation of FOXC2+ SSCs led to the depletion of the undifferentiated spermatogonia pool.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using Foxc2iCreERT2/+;Rosa26LSL-DTA/+ mice where FOXC2+ cells were ablated.

claim: During germline regeneration, FOXC2+ SSCs were activated and able to completely restore the process.
source: During germline regeneration, FOXC2+ SSCs were activated and able to completely restore the process.
evidence: This is supported by busulfan treatment experiments showing FOXC2+ cells survive and restore spermatogenesis.

claim: Germ cell-specific Foxc2 knockout resulted in an accelerated exhaustion of SSCs and eventually led to male infertility.
source: Germ cell-specific Foxc2 knockout resulted in an accelerated exhaustion of SSCs and eventually led to male infertility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice showing progressive loss of SSCs and infertility.

claim: FOXC2 prompts the expressions of negative regulators of cell cycle thereby ensures the SSCs reside in quiescence.
source: Furthermore, FOXC2 prompts the expressions of negative regulators of cell cycle thereby ensures the SSCs reside in quiescence.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag sequencing and scRNA-seq data showing FOXC2 binds to and regulates cell cycle inhibitors.

claim: The quiescent FOXC2+ SSCs are essential for maintaining the homeostasis and regeneration of spermatogenesis in adult mammals.
source: Thus, this work proposes that the quiescent FOXC2+ SSCs are essential for maintaining the homeostasis and regeneration of spermatogenesis in adult mammals.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental evidence including lineage tracing, ablation, and regeneration studies.

claim: SSCs are maintained in a homeostatic balance between self-renewal and differentiation.
source: It is critical for this process to be continuous and successful that SSCs are maintained in a homeostatic balance between self-renewal and differentiation (Sharma et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: SSCs belong to a subgroup of undifferentiated spermatogonia (uSPG) and exhibit significant heterogeneity and dynamic characteristics.
source: The SSCs, which belong to a subgroup of undifferentiated spermatogonia (uSPG), exhibit significant heterogeneity and dynamic characteristics.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by recent single-cell studies.

claim: A number of genes relatively higher expressed in primitive subfractions of uSPG have been identified including Gfra1, ID4, Ret, Eomes, Pax7, Nanos2, Shisa6, T, Pdx1, Lhx1, Egr2, and Plvap.
source: Within the population of uSPG, a number of genes relatively higher expressed in primitive subfractions have been identified and well investigated, that is, Gfra1, ID4, Ret, Eomes, Pax7, Nanos2, Shisa6, T, Pdx1, Lhx1, Egr2, and Plvap (Aloisio et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2004; Hara et al., 2014; Helsel et al., 2017; Jijiwa et al., 2008; La et al., 2018; Nakagawa et al., 2021; Oatley et al., 2007; Sada et al., 2009; Sharma et al., 2019a; Tokue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Gfra1, ID4, Eomes, Pax7, Nanos2, and Plvap are validated through lineage tracing experiments.
source: Particularly, Gfra1, ID4, Eomes, Pax7, Nanos2, and Plvap are further validated through lineage tracing experiment, which is considered to be a reliable method to study the development of stem cells.
evidence: This statement references previous lineage tracing studies in the literature.

claim: Some essential and primitive SSC subpopulations remain undiscovered.
source: However, some essential and primitive subpopulations remain undiscovered, and the identification of which is of great significance for elucidating the developmental process of SSC renewal and its behavior in testis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Adult stem cells are characteristic for a unique quiescent status reflected by both reversible cell cycle arrest and specific metabolic alterations.
source: Adult stem cells, as the undifferentiated primitive cells that can be found in nearly all types of tissues in mammals, are characteristic for a unique quiescent status reflected by both reversible cell cycle arrest and specific metabolic alterations (van Velthoven and Rando, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The role of quiescent stem cells is to avoid premature exhaustion and to allow the long-term maintenance of a functional stem cell pool.
source: The role of the quiescent stem cells is to avoid premature exhaustion and to allow the long-term maintenance of a functional stem cell pool (Cheung and Rando, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Adult SSCs are largely non-proliferative while capable of reciprocating between the quiescent and activated status during homeostasis and regeneration.
source: The adult SSCs appear to share this characteristic, as revealed in recent single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis in humans and mice, being largely non-proliferative while capable of reciprocating between the quiescent and activated status during homeostasis and regeneration (Guo et al., 2018; Hermann et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2021; Tan and Wilkinson, 2019; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent scRNA-seq studies.

claim: USF1 and DNMT3L are important regulators of SSC quiescence.
source: This notion has also been significantly supported by the discoveries of important regulators such as USF1 (Faisal et al., 2019) and DNMT3L (Liao et al., 2014) as well as the pathways including the PI3K/MAPK and mTORC1 signalings (Suzuki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PI3K/MAPK and mTORC1 signaling pathways are involved in SSC quiescence regulation.
source: This notion has also been significantly supported by the discoveries of important regulators such as USF1 (Faisal et al., 2019) and DNMT3L (Liao et al., 2014) as well as the pathways including the PI3K/MAPK and mTORC1 signalings (Suzuki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cells in a quiescent state are supposed to be more resilient to genotoxic insults.
source: In addition, it is generally believed that cells in a quiescent state are supposed to be more resilient to genotoxic insults, thus theoretically the quiescent SSCs can restore spermatogenesis upon such disturbance.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about quiescent stem cells.

claim: Much remains unknown about the characteristics and regulation of the quiescence state of adult SSCs.
source: However, by large, much remain unknown as to the characteristics and regulation of the quiescence state of adult SSCs.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: FOXC2 is a member of the forkhead/winged helix transcription factor family.
source: Forkhead box protein C2 (FOXC2), a member of the forkhead/winged helix transcription factor family, plays essential roles in the development of various tissues in mice (Bahuau et al., 2002; Kume et al., 2001; Motojima et al., 2016; Sasman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FOXC2 plays essential roles in the development of various tissues in mice.
source: Forkhead box protein C2 (FOXC2), a member of the forkhead/winged helix transcription factor family, plays essential roles in the development of various tissues in mice (Bahuau et al., 2002; Kume et al., 2001; Motojima et al., 2016; Sasman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: FOXC2 has been found to be expressed in As and Apr spermatogonia of mouse testes and is required for SSC maintenance.
source: Recently, FOXC2 has been found to be expressed in As and Apr spermatogonia of mouse testes and is required for SSC maintenance (Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The role of FOXC2 in the development of adult SSCs in vivo has yet to be explored.
source: However, the role of FOXC2 in the development of adult SSCs in vivo has yet to be explored.
evidence: This is an assessment of the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Cluster1 was characterized by the high expression of stemness markers whereas other clusters were featured by progenitor or differentiating spermatogonia (dSPG) markers.
source: Among five distinct clusters identified, Cluster1 was characterized by the high expression of stemness markers whereas other clusters were featured by progenitor or differentiating spermatogonia (dSPG) markers (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Cluster1 cells appeared quiescent and likely represented the primitive state of uSPG populations.
source: Primarily mapped to the extreme early point of the developmental trajectory, Cluster1 cells appeared quiescent and likely represented the primitive state of uSPG populations (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental trajectory analysis and cell cycle marker expression.

claim: The top 10 differentially expressed genes associated with Cluster1 are featured by SSC markers such as Mcam, Gfra1, Tcl1 and Egr2.
source: The top 10 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) associated with Cluster1 are featured by SSC markers such as Mcam (Kanatsu-Shinohara et al., 2012), Gfra1 (Hara et al., 2014), Tcl1 and Egr2 (Hermann et al., 2018; La et al., 2018; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: FOXC2 was exclusively localized in the nucleus of a subgroup of ZBTB16+ uSPG in mice.
source: in which only FOXC2 was exclusively localized in the nucleus of a subgroup of ZBTB16+ uSPG in mice (Buaas et al., 2004; Costoya et al., 2004; Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining shown in the figures.

claim: FOXC2 displayed differential expressions among various subtypes of uSPG, being more specific in As (59.9%) than other subtypes including Apr (5.2%), Apr-1 (4.1%), Aal4-1 (1.83%), Aal8-1 (1.5%), and Aal16-1 (1.67%).
source: More specifically, FOXC2 displayed differential expressions among various subtypes of uSPG, being more specific in As (59.9%) than other subtypes including Apr (5.2%), Apr-1 (4.1%), Aal4-1 (1.83%), Aal8-1 (1.5%), and Aal16-1 (1.67%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Only a small fraction (5.1%) of FOXC2+ cells are active in proliferation as indicated by MKI67.
source: There was only a small fraction (5.1%) active in proliferation as indicated by MKI67 (Figure 1F), suggesting that FOXC2+ cells are primarily quiescent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunostaining for FOXC2 and MKI67 shown in Figure 1F.

claim: FOXC2 displays a higher level of co-localization with GFRA1 and EOMES than PAX7 and NEUROG3.
source: Additionally, when examining the SSC markers validated previously by lineage tracing (La and Hobbs, 2019), we found that FOXC2 displays a higher level of co-localization with GFRA1 and EOMES than PAX7 and NEUROG3 (Nakagawa et al., 2007), indicating the FOXC2+ cells contain but differ from the known SSC subsets (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: FOXC2 was specifically expressed in human SSCs, most of which were MKI67-.
source: As expected, FOXC2 was also specifically expressed in the human SSCs, most of which were MKI67- (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of published human scRNA-seq data and immunofluorescence.

claim: FOXC2+ cells located at the start of the developmental trajectory with a proportion of about 90% that were MKI67- in human testis.
source: Pseudotime analysis showed that the FOXC2+ cells located at the start of the developmental trajectory with a proportion of about 90% that were MKI67- (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime analysis of human scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: FOXC2+ cells were a subset of ZBTB16+ spermatogonia in adult human testis, and most of them were MKI67-.
source: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that FOXC2+ cells were a subset of ZBTB16+ spermatogonia in adult human testis, and most of them were MKI67- (Figure 1J), representing a quiescent subpopulation of SSCs in human testis (Clermont, 1966a; Clermont, 1966b; Clermont, 1969; Ehmcke and Schlatt, 2006; Ehmcke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining of human testis sections shown in Figure 1J.

claim: FOXC2 is similarly expressed in the SSCs of adult human and mouse testis and may possess a conserved function.
source: These results suggest that FOXC2 is similarly expressed in the SSCs of adult human and mouse testis and may possess a conserved function.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar expression patterns observed in both human and mouse.

claim: At d3, the tracked cells were both GFP+ and FOXC2+.
source: At d3, the tracked cells were both GFP+ and FOXC2+ (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GFP+ cells constituted 0.027% of the total testicular cells at d3 after tamoxifen induction.
source: and constituted 0.027% of the total testicular cells as indicated by the fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FOXC2+ cells generated 3.6 times greater number of colonies than the THY1+ control in transplantation assays.
source: Two months after transplantation, FOXC2+ cells generated 3.6 times greater number of colonies than the THY1+ control (Figure 2D and E), indicating that the FOXC2+ cells possess higher stemness as convinced by stronger transplantable viability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by transplantation experiments shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: At w1, all GFP+ cells were identified as uSPGs, encompassing As, Apr, and Aal-4.
source: At w1, all GFP+ cells were identified as uSPGs, encompassing As, Apr, and Aal-4 (Figure 2Fa).
evidence: This is demonstrated by whole-mount immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FOXC2+ As gave rise to three types of Apr: FOXC2+/FOXC2+, FOXC2+/FOXC2-, and FOXC2-/FOXC2-.
source: Specifically, FOXC2+ As gave rise to three types of Apr, that is, FOXC2+/FOXC2+, FOXC2+/FOXC2-, and FOXC2-/FOXC2- (Figure 2Fc1, b, c2, d2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by lineage tracing analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FOXC2+ cells are capable of self-renewal to sustain the population as well as replenishing the uSPG pool by producing downstream progenies, thereby serving as SSCs.
source: These results confirm that FOXC2+ cells are capable of self-renewal to sustain the population as well as replenishing the uSPG pool by producing downstream progenies, thereby serving as SSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lineage tracing data showing both self-renewal and differentiation.

claim: GFP+ colonies produced GFP+ sperms in the epididymis, from which healthy GFP+ offspring were given birth by C57BL/6J female recipients.
source: In the following 2–6 weeks, GFP+ colonies further expanded and produced GFP+ sperms in the epididymis, from which healthy GFP+ offspring were given birth by C57BL/6J female recipients (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: GFP+ colonies constituted 83.67%, 90.48%, 96.78%, 98.55%, and 99.31% of the total length of the seminiferous tubules at w6, m2, m4, m7, and m12, respectively.
source: The GFP+ colonies constituted 83.67%, 90.48%, 96.78%, 98.55%, and 99.31% of the total length of the seminiferous tubules at w6, m2, m4, m7, and m12, respectively (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of lineage tracing shown in Figures 2H and 2I.

claim: All offspring were GFP+ from m4 onward.
source: All offspring were GFP+ from m4 onward (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of offspring shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The EOMES+, GFRA1+, and PAX7+ cells were all GFP+ at w2.
source: Additionally, the EOMES+, GFRA1+, and PAX7+ cells were all GFP+ at w2, further confirming these progenies were derived from the FOXC2+ cells (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2K.

claim: FOXC2+ SSCs can produce all subtypes of uSPG, thus initiating spermatogenesis in adult mice.
source: Overall, FOXC2+ SSCs can produce all subtypes of uSPG, thus initiating spermatogenesis in adult mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive lineage tracing data.

claim: Gradual loss of weight in testes coincided with the reduction in the size of testes in all the mice while body weight was maintained after FOXC2+ cell ablation.
source: Gradual loss of weight in testes coincided with the reduction in the size of testes in all the mice while body weight was maintained (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by measurements shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: At d14 after FOXC2+ ablation, all GFRA1+, LIN28A+, and ZBTB16+ uSPG disappeared while vacuoles formed at the basement membrane with remaining spermatocytes and spermatids in the seminiferous lumen.
source: at d14, all GFRA1+, LIN28A+, and ZBTB16+ uSPG disappeared while vacuoles formed at the basement membrane with remaining spermatocytes and spermatids in the seminiferous lumen (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and histological analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The expression of DDX4 and DAZL as germ cell markers was significantly reduced along with nearly undetectable expression of uSPG markers such as ZBTB16, LIN28A, GFRA1, RET, and NEUROG3 after FOXC2+ ablation.
source: Meanwhile, the expression of DDX4 (Toyooka et al., 2000) and DAZL (Li et al., 2019) as germ cell markers was significantly reduced along with nearly undetectable expression of uSPG markers such as ZBTB16, LIN28A, GFRA1, RET, and NEUROG3 (Nakagawa et al., 2007; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: FOXC2+ population plays a critical role in spermatogenesis.
source: These results indicate an uSPG exhaustion as the result of the FOXC2+ SSCs ablation, therefore supporting the critical role played by FOXC2+ population in spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the ablation experiments showing uSPG depletion.

claim: At d20 post busulfan treatment, FOXC2+ cells constituted the majority of uSPGs.
source: At d20 post busulfan treatment (20 mg/kg), FOXC2+ cells constituted the majority of uSPGs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Following a sharp decrease in cell number in the first 5 days after busulfan treatment, ZBTB16+ and GFRA1+ cells began to recover from d25 while the number of FOXC2+ cells remained stable.
source: Following a sharp decrease in cell number in the first 5 days, ZBTB16+ and GFRA1+ cells began to recover from d25 while the number of FOXC2+ cells remained stable (Figure 4B), indicating that this population is insensitive to busulfan.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FOXC2+ population is insensitive to busulfan.
source: Following a sharp decrease in cell number in the first 5 days, ZBTB16+ and GFRA1+ cells began to recover from d25 while the number of FOXC2+ cells remained stable (Figure 4B), indicating that this population is insensitive to busulfan.
evidence: This is inferred from the stable cell numbers after busulfan treatment.

claim: At d30 after busulfan treatment, the MKI67+ proportion in FOXC2+ cells rose to 15.92%.
source: At d30, the MKI67+ proportion rose to 15.92%, indicating a higher level of proliferation, albeit the total cell number stayed static (Figure 4B and D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunostaining analysis shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Up to d120 after busulfan treatment, the MKI67+ proportion in FOXC2+ cells had settled gradually back to the pre-treatment level, accompanied by the full recovery of spermatogenesis.
source: Up to d120, the MKI67+ proportion had settled gradually back to the pre-treatment level, accompanied by the full recovery of spermatogenesis (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At d20 after busulfan treatment, the survived uSPGs were predominantly GFP+ in lineage tracing experiments.
source: Consistent with the results above, at d20, the survived uSPGs were predominantly GFP+ (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lineage tracing shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Over 68.5% of the total length of the seminiferous tubules were GFP+ at m2 after busulfan treatment, and this proportion rose to 95.43%, 98.41%, and 99.27% at m4, m7, and m12, respectively.
source: Over 68.5% of the total length of the seminiferous tubules were GFP+ at m2, and this proportion rose to 95.43%, 98.41%, and 99.27% at m4, m7, and m12, respectively (Figure 4G and H)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of lineage tracing shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: From m4 onward after busulfan treatment, nearly all germ cells, spermatids, and their offspring were GFP+.
source: From m4 onward, nearly all germ cells, spermatids, and their offspring were GFP+ (Figure 4G, I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lineage tracing analysis shown in Figures 4G and 4I.

claim: FOXC2+ SSCs are indispensable for germline regeneration that is central to spermatogenesis recovery from interruptions.
source: Together, these results confirm that FOXC2+ SSCs are indispensable for germline regeneration that is central to spermatogenesis recovery from interruptions.
evidence: This is concluded from the busulfan treatment and lineage tracing experiments.

claim: No significant difference was observed in the expressions of various uSPG markers, including ZBTB16 and LIN28A, between Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ and Foxc2f/+ mice at the age of 1 week.
source: No significant difference was observed in the expressions of various uSPG markers, including ZBTB16 and LIN28A, between Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ and Foxc2f/+ mice at the age of 1 week (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Adult Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice displayed clear testis weight loss without significant body weight loss.
source: However, adult Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice displayed clear testis weight loss without significant body weight loss (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by measurements shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: In Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice, severe degeneration of seminiferous tubules, reduced number of spermatids in the epididymis, and decreased size of the uSPG population with age were observed.
source: Moreover, in these mice, we observed severe degeneration of seminiferous tubules, reduced number of spermatids in the epididymis, and decreased size of the uSPG population with age (Figure 5D–G) but without apparent signs of apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological and immunofluorescence analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The 6-month-old Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice were infertile, in which over 95% seminiferous tubules were Sertoli-only with hardly detectable expressions of DAZL, DDX4, LIN28A, and ZBTB16.
source: The 6-month-old Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice were infertile, in which over 95% seminiferous tubules were Sertoli-only with hardly detectable expressions of DAZL, DDX4, LIN28A, and ZBTB16 (Figure 5D–F and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis and qRT-PCR shown in the figures.

claim: FOXC2 is essential for maintaining the SSC homeostasis and normal spermatogenesis in adult mice.
source: Therefore, FOXC2 is essential for maintaining the SSC homeostasis and normal spermatogenesis in adult mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the Foxc2 knockout experiments showing progressive SSC loss and infertility.

claim: Cluster1 represented the FOXC2-expressing SSCs in Foxc2f/+ mice corresponding to the FOXC2-deleting SSCs in the Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice.
source: The pseudotime analysis identified Cluster1, which represented the FOXC2-expressing SSCs in Foxc2f/+ mice corresponding to the FOXC2-deleting SSCs in the Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice, was specifically assigned to the extremely early stage of the development trajectory in respective samples, which was validated by the expression of corresponding markers (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Cells derived from Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice were specifically associated with the late stage of the development trajectory, as opposed to Foxc2f/+ mice where nearly all the cells derived were concentrated at the early stage of development.
source: Aggregated analysis of the overall uSPG populations showed that cells derived from Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice were specifically associated with the late stage of the development trajectory, as opposed to Foxc2f/+ mice where nearly all the cells derived were concentrated at the early stage of development (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pseudotime analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The loss of FOXC2 prompts the SSCs to progress into a more differentiated stage.
source: This implies that the loss of FOXC2 prompts the SSCs to progress into a more differentiated stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the pseudotime analysis showing cells from knockout mice at later developmental stages.

claim: Subclusters0 was formed primarily by the Cluster1 cells derived from Foxc2f/+ mice and was featured by stemness markers.
source: Formed primarily by the Cluster1 cells derived from Foxc2f/+ mice, Subclusters0 was featured by stemness markers, while Subcluster1, representing the majority of Cluster1 cells from Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice, was featured by progenitor markers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcluster analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Subcluster1, representing the majority of Cluster1 cells from Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice, was featured by progenitor markers.
source: Formed primarily by the Cluster1 cells derived from Foxc2f/+ mice, Subclusters0 was featured by stemness markers, while Subcluster1, representing the majority of Cluster1 cells from Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice, was featured by progenitor markers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcluster analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: FOXC2 deletion caused defective SSC maintenance and committed the SSCs to a differentiation destiny.
source: Thus, FOXC2 deletion caused defective SSC maintenance and committed the SSCs to a differentiation destiny.
evidence: This is inferred from the scRNA-seq analysis showing cells from knockout mice at more differentiated states.

claim: There were 932 genes down-regulated in Cluster1 cells derived from Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice in comparison to Foxc2f/+ mice.
source: Further, there were 932 genes down-regulated in Cluster1 cells derived from Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice in comparison to Foxc2f/+ mice (Figure 6F, Figure 6—source data 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The down-regulated genes in Cluster1 upon Foxc2 knockout were functionally associated with both stem cell population maintenance and mitotic cell cycle.
source: which were functionally associated with both stem cell population maintenance and mitotic cell cycle (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: GSEA revealed a more progressive cell cycle in Cluster1 upon Foxc2 knockout.
source: Consistently, the gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed a more progressive cell cycle in Cluster1 upon Foxc2 knockout (Figure 6H), confirming the role of FOXC2 in regulating the cell cycle of the SSCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GSEA shown in Figure 6H.

claim: FOXC2 plays a role in regulating the cell cycle of the SSCs.
source: Consistently, the gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed a more progressive cell cycle in Cluster1 upon Foxc2 knockout (Figure 6H), confirming the role of FOXC2 in regulating the cell cycle of the SSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSEA and differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Specific peaks enriched in the promoter region of 3629 genes were identified by CUT&Tag sequencing of FOXC2+ SSCs.
source: Specific peaks enriched in the promoter region of 3629 genes (Figure 7B and C; Figure 7—source data 1) showed functional enrichment in biological processes such as DNA repair and mitotic cell cycle regulation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CUT&Tag sequencing analysis shown in the figures.

claim: FOXC2 binding peaks showed functional enrichment in biological processes such as DNA repair and mitotic cell cycle regulation.
source: Specific peaks enriched in the promoter region of 3629 genes (Figure 7B and C; Figure 7—source data 1) showed functional enrichment in biological processes such as DNA repair and mitotic cell cycle regulation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GO enrichment analysis of CUT&Tag peaks shown in Figure 7D.

claim: 306 genes were identified as candidates subjective to the regulation by FOXC2 by overlapping CUT&Tag and scRNA-seq data.
source: By overlapping with the 932 genes down-regulated in Cluster1 cells from Foxc2f/-;Ddx4Cre/+ mice, we obtained 306 genes as the candidates subjective to the regulation by FOXC2 (Figure 7E; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: GO enrichment analysis of the 306 FOXC2 target genes highlighted a distinctive functional cluster (11 genes) focusing on the negative regulation of cell cycle.
source: Further, Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of these genes highlighted a distinctive functional cluster (11 genes) focusing on the negative regulation of cell cycle (Figure 7F; Figure 7—source data 1; Bahar et al., 2002; Bakker et al., 2004; Gaudet et al., 2011; Georgescu et al., 2014; Knudson and Korsmeyer, 1997; Nitiss, 2009; Raman et al., 2007; van Oosten et al., 2005; Weaver et al., 2003; Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Significant peaks enrichment at the promoter region were observed for cell cycle negative regulator candidate genes.
source: More specifically, significant peaks enrichment at the promoter region were observed for these candidate genes (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chromatin landscape analysis shown in Figure 7G.
